title: Develop AI Security Education and Awareness
intro: Why AI skills are a security control and a legal expectation; how to run skills assessments and gap analyses for people who build, buy, operate, oversee and use AI; designing role-based AI security and ethics training; and measuring training effectiveness and a risk-aware culture.
objectives: Explain why AI literacy and competence are both a security control and a regulatory expectation
Run a skills assessment and gap analysis, prioritising gaps by risk
Design role-based AI security and ethics training for executives, builders, data teams, security operations, legal and all staff
Measure training effectiveness using reaction, learning, behaviour and results, with leading and lagging indicators
Recognise the signs of a risk-aware AI culture and avoid common measurement traps

sections.title: Skills, gaps and role-based AI training

scenes.title: Building AI-ready people
scenes.sub: Skills assessments, gap analysis and role-based training
scenes.say: Almost every control in this course depends on people: reviewers who can spot a bad output, developers who design securely, and staff who know what not to paste into a chatbot. | This video covers how to assess AI skills, find the gaps, and build training that fits each role.

scenes.title: Why AI skills are a security control

items.d: Reviewers must recognise errors and bias
What staff paste into AI tools
Deepfake voices, convincing phishing
Developers integrating models, tools and agents
The EU AI Act requires measures to support AI literacy

scenes.say: AI skills are a security control in their own right. | Human oversight only works if reviewers can recognise errors, hallucinations and bias. | Everyday data handling decides what flows into AI tools, sanctioned or not. | Staff must recognise AI-enabled deception, such as cloned voices and highly convincing phishing. | Developers integrating models, tools and agents need to know how these systems are attacked. | And there is a legal expectation: the EU AI Act requires providers and deployers to take measures supporting the AI literacy of their staff and others using AI on their behalf.

scenes.title: Running a skills gap analysis
scenes.say: A skills gap analysis has six steps. First, define the roles that interact with AI, and the competencies each needs, ideally in a competency framework. | Assess current skills, using knowledge tests and, better, practical exercises, rather than self-rating alone. | Map the gaps by role and team, so you can see where the shortfalls are. | Prioritise by risk: a gap among people who approve high-impact AI decisions matters more than one among occasional users. | Close the gaps by training, hiring or partnering with specialists. | And reassess regularly, because AI tools and threats change faster than most skills frameworks.

scenes.title: Typical competencies and gaps by role
rows: Treating AI risk as purely technical
Secure AI design, threat modelling, LLM risks
Trusting model output; over-broad agent permissions
No playbooks for prompt injection or poisoning
Acceptable use, data handling, spotting deception
Pasting sensitive data into public tools
scenes.say: Competencies and gaps differ by role. | Executives and boards need to understand AI risk, accountability and risk appetite. A common gap is treating AI risk as a purely technical matter. | Developers and machine learning engineers need secure AI design, threat modelling and knowledge of LLM-specific risks. Common gaps are trusting model output and giving agents over-broad permissions. | Security operations teams need to read AI telemetry and respond to AI incidents. A common gap is having no playbooks for prompt injection or data poisoning. | And all staff need acceptable use, data handling and the ability to spot AI-enabled deception. The most common gap is pasting sensitive data into public tools.

Secure AI engineering, labs, threat modelling

scenes.say: A role-based programme might look like this. | Short, scenario-based briefings for the board and executives on AI risk, legal duties and appetite. | Hands-on secure AI engineering for builders, with labs and threat modelling. | Data governance, privacy, bias and poisoning for data teams. | Detection, response and red-teaming skills for security operations. | AI contracts, due diligence and intellectual property for procurement and legal. | And for all staff, safe use and reporting, plus deeper training for anyone with human oversight duties.

scenes.title: Training that changes behaviour

items.h: Specific to the role and tools
items.d: Use the systems and policies people actually work with
Exercises beat slides
Prompts and tips at the point of use
AI changes in months, not years

scenes.say: Training that actually changes behaviour shares four features. | It is specific to the role, and uses the tools and policies people actually work with. | It is practical and scenario-based: a realistic exercise teaches more than a slide deck. | It is short, frequent and delivered just in time, for example a reminder inside the AI tool when someone is about to paste sensitive data. | And it is refreshed often, because AI tools and threats change in months, not years.

items: People are the control: oversight, data handling, secure building
Gap analysis: roles, assess, map, prioritise, close, reassess
Train by role: board, builders, data, SecOps, legal, all staff
scenes.say: To recap. | People are a control: they provide oversight, handle data and build systems. | A gap analysis defines roles, assesses skills, maps and prioritises gaps by risk, closes them and reassesses. | Train by role: board, builders, data teams, security operations, procurement and legal, and all staff. | And make training practical, specific, frequent and regularly refreshed.

blocks.md:
### AI literacy as an obligation and a control
Article 4 of the **EU AI Act** requires providers and deployers to take measures to support the **AI literacy** of their staff and other people operating or using AI systems on their behalf, taking into account their technical knowledge, experience, education and training and the context of use. The 2026 Digital Omnibus softened the wording (organisations must support literacy rather than guarantee a sufficient level), but it still applies, and national authorities enforce it. ISO/IEC 42001 similarly requires the organisation to determine and ensure the **competence** of people doing AI-related work (clause 7.2) and to make people **aware** of the AI policy and their contribution (clause 7.3).

From a security perspective, skills matter because people are part of most AI controls: they configure systems, approve outputs, review decisions, handle data, respond to incidents and recognise deception.

### Skills assessments and gap analysis
1. **Define roles and competencies.** Identify every role that builds, buys, operates, oversees or uses AI, and the competencies each needs. A simple competency framework might have levels (aware, practitioner, expert) across areas such as AI concepts, AI risk and governance, secure AI engineering, data protection, AI threat detection and response, and responsible AI.
2. **Assess current capability** using a mix of methods: knowledge assessments; practical exercises (for example, reviewing AI outputs for errors, threat-modelling a RAG design, triaging a simulated AI incident); work-product review; certifications; and self-assessment (useful but optimistic).
3. **Map gaps** in a role-by-competency heat map, by team.
4. **Prioritise by risk:** gaps among people who approve high-impact AI decisions, build agents with tool access, or handle sensitive data are urgent; gaps among occasional low-risk users are less so.
5. **Close gaps** through training, coaching, hiring, rotation or specialist partners, with owners and deadlines.
6. **Reassess** at least annually and when tools, threats or responsibilities change.

### Role-based training
| Audience | Focus | Format |
|---|---|---|
| Board and executives | AI strategy and risk, accountability, risk appetite, regulatory duties, questions to ask management | Short briefings, tabletop scenarios |
| AI governance committee, risk and compliance | Frameworks (EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001), assessments, tiering | Workshops, case studies |
| Developers and ML engineers | Secure AI architecture, OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications, threat modelling, secure use of agents and tools, supply-chain hygiene | Hands-on labs, code reviews, secure patterns |
| Data scientists and data engineers | Data governance and lineage, privacy techniques, bias evaluation, poisoning and integrity | Labs and checklists |
| Security operations | AI telemetry, detection use cases, AI incident playbooks, forensics, red teaming | Simulations, purple-team exercises |
| Procurement, legal and privacy | AI due diligence, contract terms, IP and data rights, DPIAs and FRIAs | Guides, templates, case reviews |
| Human overseers and reviewers | System capabilities and limits, automation bias, when and how to override or escalate | Scenario practice on real cases |
| All staff | Acceptable use, data classification, approved tools, verifying outputs, recognising AI-enabled scams and deepfakes, reporting | Short modules, nudges, campaigns |

### Making training effective
- **Role-specific and contextual:** use the organisation’s own tools, policies and examples.
- **Practical:** exercises and simulations change behaviour more than lectures.
- **Little and often:** microlearning and just-in-time prompts (for example, a warning in the browser when sensitive data is pasted into an AI tool) beat a single annual course.
- **Current:** refresh content as tools, attacks and regulations change, and brief people on emerging threats such as new deepfake scams.
- **Linked to consequences and support:** clear policies, accessible AI champions, and a no-blame route for reporting mistakes.

blocks.title: Match the audience to the training
pairs: Briefings on AI risk appetite, accountability and regulatory duties
Hands-on labs on threat modelling and least-privilege tool design
Simulations of AI incident triage and response
Claims reviewers overseeing an AI model
Practice spotting model errors and automation bias, and using override
Acceptable use, data handling and recognising deepfake scams

blocks.title: Prioritise by risk
blocks.md: When a question asks which group to train **first**, choose the one whose AI-related decisions carry the **highest risk**: people with human oversight duties over high-impact systems, builders of agents with tool access, or staff handling regulated data, rather than the largest group or the most senior.

q.q: A gap analysis shows that reviewers approving AI-recommended loan decisions can’t explain the model’s limitations and approve 99% of recommendations. What should be prioritised?
o: Generic AI awareness training for the whole company, so everyone shares the same baseline knowledge
Targeted training for reviewers on the model’s limits, automation bias and when to override, then reassessment
Replacing the human reviewers with a second model that checks the first model’s recommendations
Postponing training until the annual cycle, when reviewers can attend a full certification course
q.why: Reviewers provide oversight of high-impact decisions, so their gap is the highest risk. Targeted, practical training with reassessment addresses it directly.

sections.title: Measuring training effectiveness and risk-aware culture

scenes.title: Is the training working?
scenes.sub: Measuring learning, behaviour and a risk-aware AI culture
scenes.say: A hundred per cent completion rate tells you that everyone clicked through the course. It doesn’t tell you whether anyone behaves differently. | This video covers how to measure whether AI security training works, and what a risk-aware AI culture looks like in data.

scenes.title: Four levels of evaluation

layers.label: Level 4 · Results
layers.sub: Did AI risk actually fall? Incidents, leaks, audit findings

layers.label: Level 3 · Behaviour
layers.sub: Do people act differently? Tool use, DLP events, simulations

layers.label: Level 2 · Learning
layers.sub: Did they gain knowledge and skill? Assessments and practicals

layers.label: Level 1 · Reaction
layers.sub: Did they find it relevant and engaging? Surveys

scenes.say: A widely used model, from Kirkpatrick, evaluates training at four levels, and each level is harder to measure, and more valuable. | Level four is results: did AI-related risk actually fall? Look at incidents, data leaks and audit findings. | Level three is behaviour: do people act differently? Look at use of sanctioned tools, data loss prevention events and simulation results. | Level two is learning: did people gain knowledge and skill, as shown by assessments and practical exercises? | And level one is reaction: did people find the training relevant and engaging? Most programmes stop here, which is why they can’t show impact.

scenes.title: Leading and lagging indicators

items.d: Practical assessment scores, not just completion
Share of AI use through approved tools
AI mistakes, near misses and suspicious content reported
Deepfake and AI-phishing exercises
DLP alerts involving AI tools
AI incidents traced to skills or behaviour

scenes.say: Use both leading and lagging indicators. Leading indicators show whether risk is likely to fall. | Competence by role, measured with practical assessments rather than completion. | Adoption of sanctioned AI tools, as a share of all AI use. | Reporting rates for AI mistakes, near misses and suspicious content. Rising reports usually signal a healthier culture, not a worse one. | And results from deepfake and AI-phishing simulations. Lagging indicators confirm what actually happened. | Sensitive-data events involving AI tools, caught by data loss prevention. | And AI incidents whose root cause was a skills or behaviour gap.

scenes.title: What success can look like

series.n: Sensitive data pasted into unsanctioned AI

scenes.say: Here is what success can look like over six quarters. Before the programme, sensitive data is regularly pasted into unsanctioned AI tools. | In the second quarter, role-based training launches, together with an approved enterprise AI tool, and the risky behaviour starts to fall. | Meanwhile, reports of AI near misses rise steadily. That is not a sign of more problems. It shows that people now recognise issues, and trust that reporting them is safe.

scenes.title: Signs of a risk-aware AI culture

items.d: Mistakes and near misses surface early

items.h: AI is registered before it is used
items.d: Teams come to governance, not around it
Challenging the AI is normal and valued
It appears in reviews, plans and decisions

scenes.say: Culture shows up in behaviour. | People report AI mistakes and near misses without fear of blame, so problems surface early. | Teams register AI use cases before they start, coming to governance rather than going around it. | Overrides are respected: challenging an AI recommendation is normal and valued, not seen as slowing things down. | And leaders routinely ask about AI risk in reviews, plans and investment decisions.

scenes.title: Measurement traps

items.d: Finishing a course proves attendance, not skill
Satisfaction scores alone
Blame drives problems underground
Measure continuously, and segment by role

scenes.say: Avoid four measurement traps. | Treating completion as competence: finishing a course proves attendance, not skill. | Vanity metrics such as satisfaction scores on their own. | Punishing people who report mistakes, which drives problems underground and makes your metrics look better while risk grows. | And annual snapshots. Measure continuously, segment by role and team, and compare against a baseline taken before the programme began.

items: Evaluate reaction, learning, behaviour and results
Track leading and lagging indicators by role
Rising near-miss reports usually signal a healthier culture
Completion is not competence; never punish reporting
scenes.say: To recap. | Evaluate training at four levels: reaction, learning, behaviour and results. | Track leading and lagging indicators, segmented by role. | Rising reports of near misses usually signal a healthier culture, not a worse one. | And remember: completion is not competence, and punishing people who report problems destroys the data you need.

blocks.md:
### Evaluating training: the Kirkpatrick model
| Level | Question | AI security measures |
|---|---|---|
| **1 · Reaction** | Did participants find it relevant and engaging? | Post-course surveys, relevance ratings, comments |
| **2 · Learning** | Did they gain knowledge and skills? | Pre- and post-assessments; practical tasks such as identifying flawed AI outputs or threat-modelling a design |
| **3 · Behaviour** | Do they apply it at work? | Share of AI use through sanctioned tools; DLP events involving AI; override and escalation behaviour of reviewers; secure design review findings; simulation results |
| **4 · Results** | Did organisational risk fall? | AI-related incidents and their costs; data-leak events; audit findings; regulatory issues; time to detect and contain AI incidents |

Levels 3 and 4 are harder to measure but are the ones that matter to a board. Establish a **baseline** before the programme, set **targets**, and **segment** results by role, team and system, so that improvement efforts go where the risk is.

### Indicators
**Leading indicators** (predictive):
- practical competence scores by role, and the proportion of people with oversight duties who have passed role-specific training;
- adoption of sanctioned AI tools versus detected shadow AI;
- reporting rates for AI errors, near misses and suspicious content (deepfakes, AI-generated phishing);
- results of simulations, such as voice-clone payment requests or AI-themed phishing;
- time to approve AI use-case requests (slow governance drives shadow AI);
- questions raised with AI champions.

**Lagging indicators** (outcomes):
- AI incidents, categorised by root cause (skills, process, technology);
- sensitive-data exposures through AI tools;
- audit and assessment findings related to human oversight or secure development;
- policy exceptions and violations.

### Measuring culture
Risk-aware culture is visible in behaviour and in surveys:
- **Psychological safety:** people say they would report an AI mistake they made, and believe they wouldn’t be blamed.
- **Governance engagement:** proportion of AI use cases registered before use rather than discovered afterwards.
- **Challenge:** reviewers override when appropriate, and overrides are analysed rather than discouraged.
- **Leadership attention:** AI risk is discussed in management reviews, investment decisions and board reporting.

Short, regular **pulse surveys** combined with behavioural data give a more reliable picture than an annual questionnaire.

### Pitfalls
- **Completion rates as the headline metric:** they measure attendance, not capability.
- **Unintended incentives:** if teams are penalised for reported incidents, reporting falls and risk is hidden.
- **One-size-fits-all metrics:** a developer’s secure-design competence and a sales team’s data-handling behaviour need different measures.
- **No link to action:** metrics should trigger targeted interventions (for example, extra coaching for a team with rising DLP events), not just appear in a dashboard.

blocks.title: Metric examples by audience
items: **Show:** trend in AI incidents and data-leak events; proportion of high-risk AI systems whose overseers are trained and assessed; shadow AI trend; major audit findings. **Avoid:** raw completion percentages.
**Show:** findings per AI design review; time to fix AI-specific vulnerabilities; lab assessment scores; adoption of secure patterns (for example, least-privilege tool scopes).
**Show:** practical assessment results on spotting model errors; override and escalation rates compared with expected ranges; quality sampling of their decisions.
**Show:** sensitive-data events involving AI tools; sanctioned tool adoption; simulation pass rates; reporting rates.

blocks.title: Best evidence of effectiveness
blocks.md: If asked for the **best** evidence that AI security training is effective, prefer **behaviour and results** (fewer sensitive-data events, better simulation results, fewer incidents with human causes, appropriate overrides) over **reaction or completion** (satisfaction scores, percentage of staff who finished the course).

q.q: Which metric provides the BEST evidence that an AI acceptable-use training programme has changed behaviour?
o: 98% of staff completed the course within the deadline, up from 85% the previous year
Average course satisfaction rose to 4.6 out of 5, with most staff rating it highly relevant
Sensitive-data events involving unsanctioned AI tools fell by 70%, while approved tool use rose
The course was translated into ten languages, so every office could take it in its own language
q.why: Behavioural and outcome measures (Kirkpatrick levels 3 and 4) show real change. Completion, satisfaction and translation are inputs or reactions.

quiz.q: Which assessment method gives the MOST reliable picture of a reviewer’s ability to oversee an AI system?
o: Self-rating questionnaires about confidence with AI
Practical exercises reviewing realistic AI outputs for errors and bias
Course completion records for mandatory AI training
Years of experience in the role, in the organisation and with similar AI systems
quiz.why: Practical exercises show what people can actually do. Self-ratings tend to be optimistic, and completion records show attendance only.

quiz.q: In a skills gap analysis, how should gaps be prioritised?
o: By how many people in each team lack AI training
By the risk of the AI-related decisions and activities each role performs
By the size of each team, so the largest groups are trained first
By seniority, starting with executives and working down to front-line staff
quiz.why: Gaps among people overseeing high-impact systems, building agents or handling regulated data carry the most risk.

quiz.q: What does Article 4 of the EU AI Act expect of providers and deployers?
o: That every employee who uses AI holds a recognised AI certification
That they take measures to support the AI literacy of staff and others using AI for them
That AI training is delivered by accredited trainers approved by the national regulator
That staff complete a fixed number of hours of AI training each year, recorded centrally
quiz.why: Article 4, as amended by the 2026 Omnibus, requires measures to support AI literacy, taking into account people’s knowledge, experience and context of use.

quiz.q: Which training is MOST appropriate for ML engineers building agents with tool access?
o: A general video on what AI is and how large language models work
Hands-on labs in threat modelling, secure tool integration and least privilege
A board-level briefing on the organisation’s AI risk appetite and governance
Annual phishing awareness training, refreshed with examples of AI-written emails
quiz.why: Builders need practical, role-specific skills for the risks they create, such as excessive agency and insecure tool integration.

quiz.q: Which feature MOST improves the behavioural impact of AI awareness training?
o: A single comprehensive annual course that covers every AI policy in depth
Short, scenario-based, role-specific content with just-in-time prompts at the point of use
Generic content identical for all roles, so that every employee hears the same message
Content that stays unchanged from year to year, so staff can easily compare their progress
quiz.why: Practical, contextual and frequent training changes behaviour; one-off generic courses rarely do.

quiz.q: In the Kirkpatrick model, which level measures whether people apply what they learned at work?
o: Level 1: Reaction
Level 2: Learning
Level 3: Behaviour
Level 4: Results
quiz.why: Level 3 measures on-the-job behaviour, for example DLP events or use of sanctioned tools; level 4 measures organisational results.

quiz.q: After an AI awareness campaign, reports of AI near misses rise sharply. What does this MOST likely indicate?
o: The campaign increased risk by encouraging more staff to experiment with AI tools
Improved recognition and trust in reporting, a sign of a healthier safety culture
The reporting system is malfunctioning and logging the same events more than once
Staff are over-reporting minor issues to show compliance with the new campaign
quiz.why: More reporting typically reflects better awareness and psychological safety; incidents were probably happening before but went unreported.

quiz.q: Which is a leading indicator of AI security risk among staff?
o: The number of regulatory fines received last year
The share of AI use going through sanctioned tools
The total cost of the most recent AI incident
The number of findings in last year’s audit report
quiz.why: Leading indicators predict future risk. Sanctioned-tool adoption signals reduced shadow-AI exposure; fines, costs and past findings are lagging.

exam.q: An organisation plans AI training for 8,000 staff but has a limited budget. A gap analysis shows the most serious gaps among 40 claims reviewers who oversee a high-impact AI model. What is the BEST plan?
o: Spread the budget evenly across all 8,000 staff, so everyone receives the same training standard
Prioritise intensive, practical training for the 40 reviewers, with lighter awareness for everyone else
Train executives first, so that leadership can cascade AI knowledge down through the organisation
Delay training until the budget increases, so the programme can be delivered properly to all staff
exam.why: Risk-based prioritisation focuses resources where gaps matter most, while still providing baseline awareness for all staff.

exam.q: A company’s AI training is a single 60-minute generic module each year. Shadow AI and data-leak events remain high. Which change is MOST likely to help?
o: Extend the annual module to 120 minutes, so that it covers every AI policy and approved tool in much more detail
Role-specific, scenario-based modules, just-in-time prompts in AI tools, and an approved tool with guidance
Remove training and rely on blocking every unapproved AI website at the network perimeter
Require staff to re-sign the AI policy twice a year, with managers tracking who has not signed
exam.why: Behaviour changes when training is relevant, practical and delivered at the point of use, and when people have a sanctioned alternative.

exam.q: The board asks for evidence that the AI security awareness programme reduces risk. Which report BEST answers the question?
o: Course completion of 99% across the organisation, with all overdue staff followed up by managers
Trends in AI data events, simulation results and human-caused incidents against the pre-programme baseline
Average satisfaction of 4.7 out of 5, with most staff saying the training was relevant to their role
The number of training sessions delivered, broken down by business unit, region and job family
exam.why: Behaviour and results measures, against a baseline, show whether risk changed. Completion, satisfaction and activity counts don’t.

exam.q: A manager proposes disciplining every employee who reports pasting confidential data into an AI tool by mistake. What is the MOST likely effect?
o: Fewer actual incidents, because staff will become more careful
Fewer reports while incidents continue unseen, harming culture and metrics
Better training completion, because staff will want to avoid disciplinary action
Little effect, because most employees already report mistakes voluntarily
exam.why: Punishing self-reporting drives incidents underground. A no-blame reporting route, combined with coaching and technical controls, preserves visibility.
